history.heading: Melanesia meets Polynesia
paragraphs: Fiji, an archipelago of over 300 islands in the South Pacific, was settled around 3,000 years ago by people of the Lapita culture. Fijian society developed powerful chiefdoms and had close contacts with Tonga and Samoa, blending Melanesian and Polynesian influences.

European traders came for sandalwood and sea cucumbers in the 19th century, followed by missionaries. Chief Seru Epenisa Cakobau sought to unify the islands and, facing debts and instability, ceded Fiji to Britain in 1874.

history.heading: Colony and indentured labour
paragraphs: From 1879 to 1916, the British brought around 60,000 indentured labourers from India to work on sugar plantations. Most stayed, and their descendants, Indo-Fijians, became a large part of the population. Colonial policies protected indigenous Fijian land ownership.

history.heading: Independence and coups
paragraphs: Fiji became independent on 10 October 1970. Tensions between indigenous Fijians and Indo-Fijians shaped politics. Military coups occurred in 1987, after the election of an Indo-Fijian-led government, in 2000 and in 2006, when Commodore Frank Bainimarama took power.
A new constitution in 2013 established equal citizenship for all Fijians, and elections were held in 2014. In 2022 a peaceful change of government took place.

culture.heading: Fijian life
paragraphs: English, Fijian and Fiji Hindi are official languages. Indigenous Fijians are mostly Christian, especially Methodist, while most Indo-Fijians are Hindu, with Muslim and Sikh minorities.

Kava (yaqona), a drink made from a root, is central to ceremonies and social gatherings. Lovo is food cooked in an earth oven. Rugby is a national passion; Fiji's sevens team won Olympic gold in 2016 and 2020.

politics.heading: Parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Fiji is a parliamentary republic with a president as head of state and a prime minister leading the government, responsible to a single-chamber parliament. The military has historically played a strong role in politics.
Fiji is an influential voice in the Pacific, hosting regional organisations, and is active on climate change, which threatens low-lying coastal communities.

economy.heading: Tourism and sugar
paragraphs: Fiji has one of the more developed economies in the Pacific. Tourism is the largest industry, with visitors mainly from Australia and New Zealand. Sugar, once dominant, has declined, while bottled Fiji Water, fish, timber and garments are significant exports. Remittances are important.
The currency is the Fijian dollar. Cyclones and climate change are major risks.
